name: Confucius
summary: Confucius wrote no treatise; his views come from the Analects, compiled by disciples, and are tier-4 ancient accounts. They show a teacher who urges government by moral example over penal law, filial piety as the root of virtue, and care for inherited ritual, while praising simple living and refusing to withdraw from public life. Most modern statements are not addressed, so those answers are null.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Analects 7.26: he angled but did not use a net, shot but not at perching birds; 10.8 shows him eating meat. Restraint in taking animals.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Analects 15.10: banish the songs of Chang; 17.18: he hates the songs of Chang for confounding the music of the court. He wants music kept moral.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Analects 3.17 keeps a lapsed rite and 17.21 rebukes shortening mourning. He does not leave the choice of traditions to the present generation.

character-from-environment.rationale: Analects 17.2: by nature men are nearly alike; by practice they get to be wide apart. He also stresses teaching (15.38).

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Analects 4.12: acting from gain breeds much dissatisfaction; 4.16: the mean man cares for gain; 7.15: riches by unrighteousness are like a floating cloud.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Analects 14.18 credits Kwan Chung with saving China from barbarian dress; 3.5 and 9.13 treat the Chinese way as the civilizing one, though 9.13 says a superior man among rude tribes would transform them.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Analects treats Heaven as the source of his mission (9.5) and the ruler's Mandate of Heaven; SEP and IEP note that Heaven is largely naturalized.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Analects 12.11 ("let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister...") and SEP and IEP describe an ethics of role duties. Rights as such are not discussed.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Analects 2.16: attacking strange doctrines is injurious; 7.20: he did not talk of extraordinary things.

experts-over-public.rationale: Analects 8.9: the people can be made to follow a path but not to understand it; 16.2: when right principles prevail there are no discussions among the common people; 2.19: advance the upright.

filial-duty.rationale: Analects 2.7: filial piety today means mere support, but even dogs and horses are supported, so there must be reverence; 1.2 makes filial piety the root of goodness; 17.21 defends the three-year mourning.

gradual-change.rationale: Analects 13.17: do not desire quick results; 13.12: even a true king would need a generation for goodness to prevail.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: Analects 17.16: the failings of the ancients were better than those of the present; 15.25: "alas, there are no such things now". He looks back to Yao, Shun and Yu (8.18-8.20, 20.1).

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Analects 7.26 and 10.8: he fished, hunted with restraint and ate meat; 10.12 asks about the man hurt in the stable, not the horses.

natural-rulers.rationale: Analects 16.9 ranks those born knowing highest, but he denies being one (7.19), and 17.2 says men are near alike by nature. Rulers come through learning, not birth aptitude.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Analects 13.9: the ruler should enrich the people and then instruct them. Government has the positive task of moral teaching, far beyond protecting from violence.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Analects 6.3: the superior man helps the distressed, he does not add to the wealth of the rich; 14.45: he cultivates himself to give rest to all the people.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: Analects 13.4: asked about farming, he sends Fan Ch'ih away and calls him a small man; superior men attend to ritual, righteousness and good faith.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Analects 3.17: he keeps the sheep sacrifice that Tsze-kung wished to drop ("you love the sheep, I love the ceremony"); 3.14 and 9.5 treat the cultural tradition of Zhou as entrusted to him.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Analects 2.3 prefers rule by virtue and rites over penal regulation, though it does not address standing public law directly.

restore-past-order.rationale: Analects 3.14: "I follow Chau", the dynasty that drew on the two before it; 7.1: "a transmitter, not a maker"; 15.10: use the seasons of Hsia and banish the songs of Chang. He aims to recover the rites of the early Zhou.

rule-by-example.rationale: Analects 2.3: led by laws and punishments the people avoid punishment but have no shame; led by virtue and the rules of propriety they have shame and become good. 13.6: when the prince is correct, government works without orders. 12.19: the wind bends the grass.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Analects 3.17 keeps a lapsed ceremony, 17.21 rebukes Tsai Wo for shortening mourning, and 3.14 praises the inherited culture of Zhou. He opposes discarding inherited rites.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Analects 4.16: the superior man understands righteousness, the mean man gain; 4.12: acting from the rule of gain breeds much dissatisfaction.

simple-living.rationale: Analects 7.15: with coarse rice, water and a bent arm for a pillow, joy is still found; 4.5 and 6.9 praise Hui in his poverty.

single-common-good.rationale: Analects 2.14: the superior man is catholic and no partisan; 15.21: the mean man is a partisan, not catholic.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Analects 3.14 and 2.23: each dynasty modifies what it inherits from the one before, with known additions and subtractions. Change is built on established institutions.

state-harmful.rationale: Analects 12.17 and 13.9 treat government as the proper work of rulers who make the people prosperous and then teach them. He wants good government, not none.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Analects 13.9: after enriching the people, the ruler should instruct them; 2.3: guide them by virtue and propriety. Government is to foster the good life.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Analects 16.1: do not attack Chwan-yu; if distant people are not submissive, attract them by culture and virtue.

traditional-family.rationale: Analects 1.2 makes filial and fraternal piety the root of all virtue, and 2.21 says that being filial and friendly to brothers is itself taking part in government. SEP links family roles to the whole social order.

universal-morality.rationale: Analects 13.19 and 15.5: the virtues of reverence and good faith hold even among rude tribes; 15.23: reciprocity is a rule for all of life.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Analects 18.6: "If I associate not with mankind, with whom shall I associate?"; 14.41 describes him as one who knows it is impracticable and still does it; 9.12 shows him ready to take office.

notes: Dated 551-479 BCE. Every answer rests on the Analects, which disciples compiled after his death, so none exceeds medium. Themes searched in the Analects, SEP and IEP: government and punishment, family and mourning, ritual and tradition, wealth and gain, education and nature, foreign peoples and war, office and withdrawal, rulers and regicide, music, animals. Modern topics (economy, gender, technology, sexuality, democracy) are unaddressed and null.
